name: Odyssey
info: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic attributed to Homer, composed around the 8th or 7th century BC, which follows Odysseus's ten-year journey home from the Trojan War and stands among the oldest works of literature still read.

facts.made: Attributed to Homer, whose life and authorship are debated; most scholars hold that it grew out of a long oral tradition of Greek poets and was performed by singers (aoidoi) and rhapsodes
facts.form: An epic poem in Homeric Greek of 12109 lines in dactylic hexameter, divided into 24 books
facts.where: The Greek text survives through ancient and Byzantine scholarship; the first printed edition appeared in Milan in 1488
facts.known: Odysseus's homecoming (nostos); the Cyclops Polyphemus and the name Nobody; Penelope's weaving and faithfulness; the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis; guest-friendship (xenia); the contest of the bow

t: The Odyssey grew out of an oral tradition over hundreds of years, and whether Homer lived, and when, is still debated.
Its story of Odysseus's return to Ithaca turns on homecoming, wandering, guest-friendship, testing and omens, and gives women and slaves larger roles than most ancient literature.
It was a school text across the Greek and Roman worlds and Byzantium, and its retellings run from Dante and Joyce to modern novels and films.
dyk: Penelope tests the returned Odysseus by asking to have their bed moved; only he knows it cannot be, because he carved it from the trunk of a living olive tree.
ev: The Odyssey is composed in Homeric Greek as part of a long oral tradition
The Homeric poems gain a canonical place in Athens, probably performed at the Panathenaia festival
Alexandrian scholars such as Aristarchus of Samothrace study and edit the text
Nicholas Sigeros provides Petrarch with manuscripts of the Iliad and the Odyssey
Demetrios Chalkokondyles produces the first printed edition, printed in Milan
George Chapman's translations of both epics are published together, the first complete Odyssey in English
James Joyce publishes Ulysses, a reworking of the Odyssey set in Dublin

sections.origins:
The Odyssey is one of the two major epics of ancient Greek literature attributed to Homer. It was first composed in Homeric Greek around the 8th or 7th century BC, though there is no consensus on its date. The Greeks began adapting the Phoenician alphabet during the eighth century BC, and if the Homeric poems were among the earliest products of that literacy, they would have been composed late in that century. The poems' language, however, can be dated to long before widespread literacy.

Scholars agree that the Homeric epics developed within an oral tradition over hundreds of years. Both poems assume that their audiences already knew the story of the Trojan War, which indicates that they drew on an existing body of myth. The Odyssey does not directly refer to the events the Iliad depicts, and the two are generally thought to have formed independently; it is not clear which came first.

Scholars also note strong influences from Near Eastern myth and literature. Martin West pointed to parallels with the Epic of Gilgamesh: both heroes travel to the ends of the earth and receive directions to the land of the dead from a divine woman who lives by the sea, Circe in one poem and Siduri in the other.
sections.content:
Ten years after the Achaeans won the Trojan War, Odysseus, king of Ithaca, has still not returned home. In his absence 108 suitors court his wife Penelope, who delays them by weaving a shroud for his father Laertes and secretly unweaving it each night. Guided by the goddess Athena, his son Telemachus travels to Nestor and to Menelaus in Sparta for news. Released from the nymph Calypso, Odysseus reaches the Phaeacians and tells them of his wanderings: the lotus-eaters, the cyclops Polyphemus, the bag of winds, the sorceress Circe, the visit to the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the killing of the sun god's cattle, after which all his men were lost.

Back on Ithaca, disguised as a beggar, he tests the loyalty of his household, wins the archery contest with his own bow and kills the suitors; Telemachus hangs a group of female slaves who had been sexually used by them. Penelope tests her husband with the secret of their bed before they are reunited, and Athena ends the feud with the suitors' families.

The poem opens in medias res and is told largely through speech. Its central themes include nostos (homecoming), wandering, xenia (guest-friendship), testing and omens.
sections.making:
In the early twentieth century Milman Parry and Albert Lord showed that the Homeric poems have the marks of oral poetry, which allowed even an illiterate poet to improvise long poems through formulaic language. Their fieldwork on the South Slavic epic tradition decisively showed that the texts formed as oral poetry. Scholars still disagree on how the poems emerged from that tradition, and on whether Homer lived at all; since the nineteenth century these questions have been known as the Homeric Question.

The poem is composed in dactylic hexameter, a metre of six feet, with lines of twelve to seventeen syllables that usually form a complete sentence. Its language is simple, direct and fast-paced, but literary: its vocabulary was probably never the speech of any Greek population. Long similes drawn from nature and daily life, and fixed epithets, are characteristic of it.

Because the poem was performed for audiences by an aoidos or rhapsode, its content may have varied from telling to telling. The division into 24 books was probably made long after its composition, possibly by Alexandrian scholars or rhapsodes. Some scholars regard the Telemachy, books 1 to 4, as a later addition, and the true ending has been debated since antiquity.
sections.reception:
Homer was celebrated in Greek society as a gifted and instructive poet. By the sixth century BC the Homeric poems had a canonical place in Athens, where the tyrant Peisistratos or his son Hipparchus founded the Panathenaia, a festival that probably featured performances of them. The Iliad and the Odyssey were school texts wherever Greek was spoken, and the Romans absorbed Homer into their own culture.

Scholars at the libraries of Alexandria and Pergamum studied and edited the poems, among them Zenodotus of Ephesus, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace. Allegorical readings were popular and were used to defend Homer against charges, made by the philosopher Xenophanes, that he disrespected the gods; Porphyry read the cave of the nymphs as an image of human life.

In Byzantium the epics remained school texts, and in the middle Byzantine period adults began to read them for pleasure. John Tzetzes wrote Homeric Allegories for the consort of Manuel I Komnenos, and Eustathios of Thessalonike wrote commentaries later generations treated as authoritative. In the quarrel of the Ancients and Moderns in France, Anne Dacier defended Homer against Charles Perrault and Antoine Houdar de la Motte.
sections.survival:
The poem came down through many ancient editions. Material derived from the first-century BC scholar Didymus divides them into city editions, known for Aeolis, Argos, Cyprus and Marseille, and individual editions prepared by scholars. The spread of the Greek language into the Byzantine era kept the text known; the scholar Armstrong suggests that without it the epics might have been forgotten, as Beowulf was.

In 1354 Nicholas Sigeros gave Petrarch manuscripts of the Iliad and the Odyssey, and Giovanni Boccaccio persuaded the monk Leontius Pilatus to translate them into Latin prose; he finished the Iliad and came close to finishing the Odyssey. The first printed edition was produced in 1488 by Demetrios Chalkokondyles, born in Athens and educated in Constantinople, and printed in Milan by Antonios Damilas.

Translations followed in the sixteenth century: Andreas Divus's word-for-word Latin, Girolamo Baccelli's Italian of 1582 and Salomon Certon's French of 1604. George Chapman's English Odyssey, published with his Iliad in 1616, was the first modern translation to enjoy wide success. Later versions include Dacier's French prose of 1716, Alexander Pope's of the 1720s, produced with Elijah Fenton and William Broome, and Vasily Zhukovsky's Russian of 1849.
sections.legacy:
The Odyssey and the Iliad formed the basis of education in the ancient Mediterranean, a curriculum later taken up by Western humanists, and they mark the beginning of the Western literary tradition. Edith Hall notes that the Odyssey has been regarded as the birthplace of literary fiction, and in 2018 a BBC Culture poll of experts named it literature's most enduring narrative.

Dante met Odysseus in the eighth circle of hell and gave him a new ending in which he never returns home. Some of his adventures reappear in the Arabic tales of Sinbad the Sailor. George Chapman's translation inspired John Keats's sonnet of 1816, and James Joyce's Ulysses of 1922 reworked the poem in the Dublin of his own day; Joyce's use of the myth in turn inspired Joseph Campbell's idea of the hero's journey, which most scholars today consider reductive. Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad and Madeline Miller's Circe retell it from the side of its women.

Monteverdi's opera Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria (1640) and Fauré's Pénélope (1913) set its second half to music, and films range from L'Odissea of 1911 to O Brother, Where Art Thou? The psychiatrist Jonathan Shay related the poem to the homecoming of combat veterans.

summary: The Odyssey, attributed to Homer and composed around the 8th or 7th century BC out of a long oral tradition, tells of Odysseus's ten-year journey home from Troy and his return to Penelope. Read in Greek and Roman schools and in Byzantium, printed in 1488 and translated widely, it has shaped Western literature from Dante to Joyce.
